page.title: Can You Spot It · Samantha Paras
page.meta: A web trivia game where AI writes a paragraph with planted mistakes and you find them before time runs out. Built by a team of four; I wrote the code for the current web version.
header.summary: Every round is a short paragraph of true facts about a topic you pick, with a few factual, spelling, chronology and punctuation mistakes slipped in. You find them before time runs out.
spec.role: Role: Developer. I've written the code for the current web version.
spec.team: Team: two developers, UX/UI and QA
spec.stack: Stack: Expo · React Native · TypeScript · Supabase · Edge Functions · Anthropic API
spec.status: Status: ◐ Launching mid-November · web version first
links.none: No links yet, sorry: the repo is private and the playtest build is unlisted.
why.p: The game was a teammate's idea. They wanted something you could play to kill time that still leaves you a little sharper. You can play it on your own. Friendly competition is in now too: a season leaderboard ranked by stars.
part.p: So far I've written the code for the current web version, working from the team's UX/UI design and QA testing. That has covered:
part.bullet.1: the game screens in Expo and TypeScript
part.bullet.2: Supabase for data, with database migrations and row-level security
part.bullet.3: an Edge Function that takes a vetted true-fact paragraph, asks Anthropic's API which words to change, and checks the answer before the round starts
part.bullet.5: deploying the web build to Vercel
part.bullet.6: the leaderboard, the two Daily Prompts a day, the practice round and the How to play guide
hard.p: The generator isn't reliable enough yet, especially at Intermediate and Hard difficulty and with Science topics. For now I increased the number of retries so playtesting can go on. It's a band-aid, not a fix, and I know it.
note.hard.text: Every retry is another paid API call, and those add up. Request rate limiting caps how often requests can be made, which puts a ceiling on how many calls a burst of retries can trigger.
team.p: We track work in GitHub and Jira, and a shared planning spreadsheet holds the roadmap, open questions and decision log.
learned.p1: React Native was new to me, so I worked through the code with Claude line by line, asking why something was written that way and changing what I didn't think was necessary or didn't agree with. Claude isn't perfect, and neither am I, but that back-and-forth helped me understand the code and make my own decisions.
learned.p2: On QuestKeeper, a personal project, I could decide halfway through coding that I didn't like something and just change it. Terrible idea sometimes, lol, but I definitely did it. Working with a team has taught me to slow down, make decisions together and give everyone room to do the work they specialize in.
